Thousand Islands: An Ancient Granite Bridge Thousand Islands National Park is situated on the Frontenac Arch, a geological feature much older than the islands themselves. This ridge of ancient granite connects the Canadian Shield to the Adirondack Mountains in the US. The St. Lawrence River flooded the lowlands of this 'granite bridge' after the last ice age, creating the iconic archipelago. 🇨🇦

I've been interested in the ships on the Great Lakes since I was a kid. I grew up a bit over a mile from the Detroit River and spent many hours watching the many freighters pass by one or the other of the riverfront parks. I remember vividly the events surrounding the sinking of the Edmund Fitzgerald, seen her bell and battered lifeboat at museums, explored the preserved wheelhouse of the Henry Ford II which was (with the Arthur Anderson) one of the two freighters who went back out into the storm to look for the Fitz, and participated as an official representative of my USCGAUX Flotilla in one of the yearly memorial services at Old Mariners' Church in Detroit. Obviously, I found this article on Boatnerd.com particularly interesting and look forward to reading the book discussed in the first portion of this edition when it comes out next month.

On Jan 21 1895 the wooden-hulled passenger and cargo ship Chicora disappeared on Lake Michigan. She had been docked for the winter in St. Joseph, Michigan, but her owners agreed to transport flour from Milwaukee to St. Joseph. She left St. Joseph on Jan 20 and early the next morning was ready for her return journey. It was an unusually pleasant and calm winter morning, and she departed Milwaukee just minutes prior to a message arriving, warning the captain not to depart due to a quickly dropping barometer. The winds picked up and the weather worsened quickly. Eyewitnesses claimed to have seen the ship in trouble, and when the weather finally cleared, all that was found of her were bits and pieces of debris. The 23 crew on board were never found, and the ship remains undiscovered somewhere on the bottom of Lake Michigan. Photos credit: Michigan Shipwreck Research Association

The wreck of the Northwestern sits heeled over to her starboard side135 feet below the surface of Lake Huron. Carrying a load of salt, the 115 foot freighter sank one night in 1850 after a collision with the larger Monticello, that ship’s helmsman confused by lights while the ships were attempting to pass one another and ramming the Northwestern. Photos (and a little history lesson) by Dusty Klifman.
